sonuc: was lost during a deep-diving test
tetik: a likely piping leak in the engine room at test depth
mekanizma: probable flooding from a piping joint, reactor shutdown, and ice blocking the emergency ballast blow
ders: the US Navy created the SUBSAFE programme for submarine systems
yanilgi: The crew did try to surface. The emergency air system froze, so the ballast tanks never emptied.
tartisma: The exact cause can never be fully proven. How do you fix a failure you can only reconstruct?
soru: How do you prove what happened?
sahneler: A nuclear submarine sank during a deep-diving test.
It fell past its crush depth, and all one hundred twenty nine aboard were lost.
Investigators believe a pipe joint leaked in the engine room.
The reactor shut down, and the sub lost power.
The crew tried an emergency blow of the ballast tanks.
Ice formed in the air system and blocked it.
Without that air, Thresher kept sinking.
The Navy then created the SUBSAFE programme.

baslik: The Cargo Ship That Sailed Into a Hurricane
tetik: a route that took the ship into the storm's path
mekanizma: flooding through an open scuttle, loss of propulsion, and progressive flooding in heavy seas
ders: weather routing and older-ship safety rules were tightened
yanilgi: The captain was not ignoring every forecast. He was relying partly on weather data that was hours out of date.
tartisma: The voyage data recorder captured every doubt the crew raised. How should a crew challenge a captain?
basliklar: The Ship That Sailed Into Hurricane Joaquin
sahneler: A US cargo ship sailed into a Category 3 hurricane.
The ship sank, and all thirty three crew were killed.
Its route kept it close to the hurricane's path.
Some weather updates it relied on were hours old.
Water came in through an open hatch, and the ship listed.
Then the engine lost oil pressure and stopped.
Without power, the waves took over.
Rules on weather routing and old ships were tightened.

baslik: Two Ships Watching Each Other on Radar Still Collided
sonuc: sank after colliding with another liner in fog
tetik: radar misread on both bridges in thick fog
mekanizma: collision from misinterpreted radar plots, then a severe list that disabled half the lifeboats
ders: radar training and collision rules at sea were improved
zincir: BOTH SHIPS TRACK EACH OTHER ON RADAR
yanilgi: Neither crew was blind: both watched the other ship on radar. They misjudged the plots and turned toward each other.
tartisma: Most people survived because rescue ships came fast. Is a good rescue proof of a safe design?
basliklar: Two Ships, Two Radars, One Collision
sahneler: In thick fog, the liner Stockholm rammed the Andrea Doria.
The Doria began listing, and forty six people aboard her were killed.
Both crews had been watching each other on radar.
They misjudged the plots and turned toward each other.
The list was so steep that half the lifeboats couldn't be launched.
Nearby ships rushed in and rescued most people.
The Doria sank the next morning.
Radar training and collision rules at sea were improved.

baslik: A Showboating Sail-Past Tore Open a Cruise Ship
sonuc: capsized off the island of Giglio
tetik: a close sail-past near the island at night
mekanizma: hull breach from a rock strike flooding several compartments, then a list and capsize
ders: cruise route and evacuation rules were tightened
yanilgi: The ship wasn't lost to a storm or engine failure. It was steered off its planned route to pass close to the island.
tartisma: The evacuation began long after the impact. How long should a captain wait before ordering abandon ship?
basliklar: The Sail-Past That Tore Open a Cruise Ship
sahneler: A giant cruise ship struck a rock off the Italian island of Giglio.
It flooded and rolled onto its side, and thirty two people died.
The ship had left its route to sail close to the island.
A rock tore a long gash in the hull.
Water flooded the engine rooms, and power failed.
The order to evacuate came very late.
By then, the list made many lifeboats hard to use.
Cruise routes and evacuation rules were tightened afterward.

baslik: The Storm Tore Off a Ferry's Bow Visor
sonuc: sank in the Baltic Sea during a storm
tetik: waves tearing the bow visor's locks apart
mekanizma: failure of bow visor locks, pulling open the car ramp and flooding the vehicle deck
ders: bow visor and ramp designs on ferries were strengthened
yanilgi: The visor wasn't knocked off in one blow. Repeated wave impacts broke its locks until it fell away.
tartisma: The ferry was designed for coastal waters. Was it ever meant for that sea in that weather?
basliklar: The Bow Visor That Tore Away in a Storm
soru: Coastal ferry on the open sea?
sahneler: In a Baltic storm, the ferry Estonia sank in under an hour.
Hundreds were trapped, and eight hundred fifty two people died.
Waves pounded the ship's bow visor.
Its locks broke, and the visor tore away.
As it fell, it pulled open the car ramp behind it.
The sea poured onto the car deck.
The ship listed and sank.
Bow visors and ramps on ferries were strengthened afterward.

baslik: A Leaking Torpedo Destroyed the Submarine Kursk
sonuc: sank after two explosions during an exercise
tetik: high-test peroxide leaking from a practice torpedo
mekanizma: HTP propellant decomposition exploding in the torpedo room, setting off warheads
yanilgi: No collision sank the Kursk. The investigation traced it to a leak in one of its own practice torpedoes.
tartisma: Some crew survived the blasts for hours in the stern. Should Russia have accepted foreign rescue help sooner?
basliklar: The Practice Torpedo That Destroyed a Submarine
sahneler: Two explosions tore through the Russian submarine Kursk.
It sank in the Barents Sea, and all one hundred eighteen crew died.
The first blast came from a practice torpedo.
Its fuel was high-test peroxide, which reacts violently if it leaks.
It leaked, then exploded in the torpedo room.
The fire set off warheads in a second, far bigger explosion.
Survivors in the stern waited for rescue that came too late.
Russia later retired this type of torpedo fuel.

baslik: The Warship That Sank Minutes Into Its Maiden Voyage
sonuc: capsized minutes into its maiden voyage
tetik: a gust of wind on a top-heavy hull
mekanizma: insufficient stability: too much weight high up and too little ballast below
ders: the ship is now studied as a classic lesson in stability
yanilgi: Vasa wasn't badly built. It was well made but unstable: too heavy high up and too narrow below.
tartisma: A stability test showed the problem before launch. Why do people sail anyway?
basliklar: The Top-Heavy Warship That Failed Its Own Test
sahneler: Sweden's mighty warship Vasa sank minutes into its maiden voyage.
Within minutes, a gust tipped it over and it went down.
It carried heavy guns on two decks.
Its hull was narrow, with too little ballast below.
That made it top-heavy.
Before launch, sailors running across the deck made it roll dangerously.
It sailed anyway.
Today, Vasa is a classic lesson in why stability comes first.

baslik: Henry VIII's Warship Sank With Its Gunports Open
sonuc: heeled over and sank during battle
tetik: water entering open lower gunports as the ship turned
mekanizma: heeling in a turn with open gunports close to the waterline
ders: the recovered wreck became one of the most studied ships in history
yanilgi: It likely wasn't sunk by French guns. Most evidence points to water pouring in through its own open gunports.
tartisma: The exact cause is still debated. What evidence would settle it?
basliklar: The Gunports That Let the Sea In
sahneler: King Henry the Eighth's warship Mary Rose sank in front of his eyes.
Within minutes, most of the crew were dead.
It had been turning during a battle with the French.
As it turned, the ship heeled over.
Its lower gunports were open and close to the water.
The sea poured in.
The wreck was raised centuries later and studied in detail.
It remains one of the best-studied ships in history.

baslik: A Broken Window Sank the World's Largest Oil Rig
sonuc: capsized in a storm off Newfoundland
tetik: a wave breaking a porthole in the ballast control room
mekanizma: seawater shorting the ballast control panel, followed by wrong ballast valve operation and flooding
ders: offshore rigs got better ballast system design, training and survival gear
yanilgi: The rig wasn't simply overwhelmed by waves. A broken porthole flooded its control panel and the ballast went wrong.
tartisma: Crew had little training on the ballast system. Should rigs rely on few people who know the system?
basliklar: The Porthole That Sank a Rig
sahneler: In a violent storm, the world's largest semi-submersible rig capsized.
The crew abandoned it, and all eighty four men died.
It started with one broken porthole.
Seawater flooded the ballast control panel.
The panel shorted, and valves began acting on their own.
The rig tilted forward, and water entered its chain lockers.
It rolled over before dawn.
Rig ballast systems, training and survival gear were improved.

baslik: A Hole for a Sensor Capsized an Offshore Platform
tetik: a fatigue crack from a weld around a sensor hole in a brace
mekanizma: fatigue crack from a poor fillet weld at a hydrophone opening, leading to brace and leg failure
ders: offshore structures must now survive the loss of one member
yanilgi: The storm only finished it. A fatigue crack had been growing in one brace since it was built.
tartisma: The crack began at a tiny detail added for a sensor. How small can a fatal detail be?
basliklar: Why the Alexander L. Kielland Capsized
The Sensor Hole That Sank a Platform
soru: How small can a fatal detail be?
sahneler: An accommodation platform in the North Sea suddenly capsized.
Most of the men aboard were trapped, and one hundred twenty three died.
One of its braces had snapped.
A hole had been cut in it to fit a sensor.
The weld around that hole was poor.
A fatigue crack grew from it, wave after wave.
When the brace failed, a leg broke away.
Offshore structures must now survive losing one member.

baslik: The Carbon Fibre Hull That Imploded Near the Titanic
sonuc: imploded on a dive to the Titanic
tetik: a carbon fibre hull weakened by repeated dives
mekanizma: cumulative damage and delamination in a carbon fibre composite pressure hull
ders: the case renewed calls for independent certification of deep submersibles
yanilgi: Carbon fibre is strong in tension, but it behaves very differently under the huge compression of the deep sea.
tartisma: Experts had warned about the hull before the dive. Should innovation be allowed to skip certification?
sahneler: A small submersible diving to the Titanic imploded.
It was destroyed instantly, and all five aboard were killed.
Its hull was made of carbon fibre.
Carbon fibre is superb in tension but less predictable under deep-sea pressure.
Every dive stressed the hull again.
Damage built up inside the layers.
The sub had never been independently certified.
It renewed calls for certifying every deep submersible.

baslik: The Cruise Ship Fire That Burned Off the New Jersey Coast
sonuc: burned off the coast of New Jersey
tetik: a fire in a locker spreading through wooden interiors
mekanizma: rapid fire spread through combustible panelling, aided by open doors and delayed response
ders: fire-resistant materials and fire drills became requirements on passenger ships
yanilgi: The ship's captain had died hours before the fire. The crew faced it without clear leadership.
tartisma: The cause of the fire is still disputed. Does the cause matter more than how it spread?
basliklar: The Cruise Ship Fire That Changed Ship Safety
sahneler: A cruise liner burned off the New Jersey coast.
Fire swept through the ship, and one hundred thirty seven people died.
It began in a storage locker.
The ship's interiors were full of wooden panelling.
Wind and open doors fed the fire.
The captain had died hours earlier, leaving confusion on the bridge.
The burning hull drifted onto the beach at Asbury Park.
Ships then had to use fire-resistant materials and run fire drills.

baslik: A Schooner Without Lights Sank a Lake Michigan Steamer
sonuc: sank on Lake Michigan after a collision
tetik: a schooner striking it at night in a storm
mekanizma: collision punching a hole below the paddlewheel, with rapid flooding
ders: the disaster pushed for navigation-light rules on the Great Lakes
yanilgi: The small schooner survived. The large steamer it hit broke apart and sank.
tartisma: Most victims died in the surf near the shore. How close to safety is still too far?
basliklar: The Night Collision on Lake Michigan
sahneler: On a stormy night, a schooner rammed the steamer Lady Elgin.
Within half an hour, hundreds of people were dead.
The schooner had struck it near the paddlewheel.
Water rushed into the hull.
It went down fast.
Survivors clung to wreckage in the storm.
Many were lost in the surf near shore.
It pushed for stronger navigation-light rules on the Great Lakes.
